clinicalPearls: Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae is a slender gram-positive bacillus and the cause of a zoonosis, with pigs, fish, shellfish and poultry as principal reservoirs.
Occupational exposure is characteristic, affecting butchers, abattoir workers, fishermen, fishmongers and veterinarians.
The commonest presentation is erysipeloid: a painful, well-demarcated violaceous cellulitis of the hand or finger following a penetrating injury.
The erysipeloid lesion tends to spread slowly with central clearing and rarely suppurates or causes systemic upset.
The feared complication is infective endocarditis, which characteristically affects the aortic valve and may occur even on structurally normal native valves.
The organism is intrinsically resistant to vancomycin, an important trap when treating presumed gram-positive bacteraemia empirically.
Penicillin is the agent of choice, and the organism is also susceptible to several other beta-lactams.
Diagnosis rests on culture from a deep biopsy at the advancing edge of the skin lesion or from blood cultures in systemic disease.
reference.pathophysiology: Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae is a slender, non-spore-forming gram-positive bacillus that is widely distributed in animals, especially pigs, and in the surface slime of fish and shellfish. Human infection is a zoonosis acquired by percutaneous inoculation of contaminated animal or fish material, typically through a minor puncture or abrasion of the hand during occupational handling. The organism elaborates neuraminidase and hyaluronidase and possesses a capsule that resists phagocytosis, which together facilitate spread through the dermis and produce the characteristic well-demarcated erysipeloid lesion. Most infection remains localised, but in some hosts the bacillus invades the bloodstream to cause bacteraemia with a striking predilection for the cardiac valves, particularly the aortic valve, where it can establish endocarditis even on previously normal valves. Its intrinsic resistance to vancomycin, aminoglycosides and sulphonamides is clinically important when selecting therapy.
additionalDifferentials: Streptococcal or staphylococcal cellulitis and classical erysipelas
Acute gout or another inflammatory arthritis of the hand
Tularaemia or another zoonotic inoculation infection
additionalInvestigations: Culture of a deep skin biopsy or aspirate taken from the advancing edge of the lesion
Blood cultures where systemic infection or endocarditis is suspected
Transthoracic and, if needed, transoesophageal echocardiography for suspected endocarditis
Gram stain and species identification, bearing in mind possible misidentification as other gram-positive bacilli
Antimicrobial susceptibility testing, noting intrinsic vancomycin resistance
Documentation of occupational and animal or fish exposure history
redFlags: A new or changing heart murmur, or embolic phenomena, suggesting endocarditis
Systemic upset such as fever and rigors accompanying the skin lesion
Diffuse or rapidly spreading cutaneous involvement beyond the site of inoculation
Failure to respond to empirical vancomycin given for presumed gram-positive infection
Features of septic arthritis in an inoculated digit
reference.prognosis: Localised erysipeloid is usually self-limiting and resolves promptly with appropriate antibiotics. Erysipelothrix endocarditis, though uncommon, tends to be aggressive, carries a higher mortality than many other causes of endocarditis, and frequently requires valve surgery.
pitfalls: Treating gram-positive bacteraemia empirically with vancomycin, to which Erysipelothrix is intrinsically resistant.
Relying on superficial swabs, which often fail to grow the organism, rather than a deep biopsy of the leading edge.
Dismissing the bacillus as a contaminant diphtheroid or lactobacillus and discarding a true isolate.
Overlooking endocarditis in a patient who has erysipeloid together with systemic features.
Missing the occupational exposure history that points to the diagnosis.
management: Penicillin as first-line antimicrobial therapy, with a cephalosporin, fluoroquinolone or clindamycin as alternatives in penicillin allergy
Deliberate avoidance of vancomycin and other empirical agents to which the organism is intrinsically resistant, an important trap in presumed gram-positive bacteraemia
Wound care and analgesia for the localised erysipeloid lesion, which is generally self-limiting
Blood cultures with transthoracic and, if needed, transoesophageal echocardiography where systemic infection or endocarditis is suspected
Prolonged intravenous penicillin for the aggressive aortic-valve endocarditis, with early valve surgery where indicated by valve destruction or embolic risk
Occupational prevention through protective gloves and hand hygiene for butchers, fish handlers, abattoir workers and veterinarians
